newsitem.title: PERU: Peru guerrillas defiant, hold over 140 hostages.
newsitem.headline: Peru guerrillas defiant, hold over 140 hostages.

text.p: Ignoring pleas from around the world, defiant Marxist rebels vowed on Monday to hold over 140 hostages captive over Christmas at the Japanese embassy residence in Peru unless the government met their demands.
The heavily armed guerrillas set free many of their captives on Sunday in an emotional 225-person mass exodus that included all the U.S., British and German prisoners.

But the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels said in a statement read prior to the exodus that they would not release high-ranking Peruvian government prisoners or Japanese captives until demands for the release of jailed guerrilla comrades were met.

Adding to the tension, police sources told Reuters they believed another clandestine MRTA commando unit was at large in Lima and could strike at military targets at any time if the government attacked the rebels in the residence.

The Japanese who were still held as bargaining chips in the fortified embassy residence included top local managers of big-name companies and Japanese ambassador Morihisa Aoki, the host of the ill-fated embassy reception stormed by the rebels last Tuesday.

Reflecting the grief felt in Japan, Emperor Akihito cancelled all official birthday celebrations on Monday and Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto tracked the crisis from a special war room in the Foreign Ministry fitted out with television monitors.

As families of the released hostages celebrated wildly in Lima, President Bill Clinton welcomed the freeing of all seven American captives and called for the immediate release of those still held. Pope John Paul had earlier added his voice to the appeals for an end to the hostage ordeal, now in its sixth day.
Curiously, the Red Cross said on Monday it was still trying to establish the identity of seven of the 225 people released.
Their names did not correspond to those on a master list of hostages for release but the reasons were not immediately clear, a Red Cross source said.

Peruvian leader Alberto Fujimori has so far refused all the MRTA demands and has cut off water and electricity to the residence -- something that released hostages said was endangering the health and safety of those still inside.
"It is extremely important that water is restored," released hostage Victor Lucero told local television. "Water is indispensable. Without it, the situation is very dangerous."
Himself a doctor, Lucero said captives had developed at least eight cases of eye infections because of the foul conditions.
The MRTA statement also warned the government that "if Mr. Fujimori decides on a military solution, he will always find a Tupac Amaru member vigilant."

Police -- who have prepared commandos to storm the residence as a last resort if talks fail -- say the guerrillas include four sharpshooters at strategic windows armed with telescopic night sight rifles.

Reinforcing the rebel threat, a red-and-white Peruvian flag, decorated with a gun, a hammer, and an image of the head of Tupac Amaru -- an Indian leader who led an 18th-century uprising against Spanish conquerors before being captured and torn limb from limb by horses -- hung provocatively from a residence window on Monday.
About 900 policemen surrounded the residency on Monday, the same number who have kept guard throughout the crisis. Salads, chicken and desserts were taken in to feed the captives.

President Fujimori made a brief visit to tour the scene on Monday with his Interior Minister, but neither of the men got out of their bullet-proofed vehicle and only peeked briefly from a rolled-down window, witnesses said.

Led by Nestor Cerpa Cartolini, 43-year-old textile factory worker turned revolutionary, the mostly young rebels stormed from jungle obscurity onto the world's front pages with their surprise assault last Tuesday night.

Though police describe Cerpa as a "vicious terrorist" with a long history of bloody attacks, the rebels appear to have treated their captives well and tried to present an image of concerned social crusaders that belies their violent tactics.
Although the government has publicly rejected all their demands, the rebels said they had released most of their captives for humanitarian reasons before Christmas.
In tumultuous scenes late on Sunday, the released men filed out one-by-one to the cheers and applause of more than a thousand waiting relatives, journalists and officials.

Those released included the ambassadors of Guatemala, Honduras, Panama, Venezuela and Cuba, as well as diplomats from Bolivia, the European Union, the United Nations, Britain, Spain, Germany and the U.S. officials.
"Daddy, Daddy," shouted one young Asian girl on a man's shoulder as she finally recognised her father in one of the buses. Others wept or cried out in joy.
"I am here to thank God because he freed my brother last night, but I am staying until they all come out," said Enrique Selada, outside the residency with a candle on Monday morning.

"The worst thing really was the lack of any information, and not knowing from hour to hour what might be going on outside, what sort of negotiations might be being done," said released hostage Lucho Sakode, 47.
"But we were all happy that our wives had been freed first and that at least they were okay. That kept me going."
